note.text: A planned system relies substantially on central decisions about resource allocation and production. Planners may set targets, direct inputs and decide priorities. Public ownership is often important in the textbook model. Planning can coordinate large projects or priorities, but requires information about needs, resources and trade-offs. Weak information or incentives can lead to mismatches between targets and actual needs. Discuss the model without assuming that every public project makes an economy fully planned.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: A planned system relies substantially on central decisions about resource allocation and production. Planners may set targets, direct inputs and decide priorities. Public ownership is often important in the textbook model. Planning can coordinate large projects or priorities, but requires information about needs, resources and trade-offs. Weak information or incentives can lead to mismatches between targets and actual needs. Discuss the model without assuming that every public project makes an economy fully planned.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: An imagined planning office allocates equipment to food production and housing under a common plan. It must decide what to make, how to use resources and who receives output. If information about local needs is poor, the plan can produce too much of one item and too little of another. This is a hypothetical model, not a claim about a particular government's current arrangements.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify the decision maker and the instructions given. Compare intended priorities with the information needed to meet them. Consider both coordination benefits and the risks of rigid targets. Avoid the claim that money, choice or local planning must vanish in every economy using planning.
